text: Course six introduced Scripted REST APIs mechanically — one API, one Resource, one script, enough to build a single working GET endpoint. This lesson goes past that single-endpoint mental model into how a real Scripted REST API is actually shaped once it has more than one Resource, more than one method, and real access control to worry about.

Query parameters are how optional filters get passed without cluttering the path. request.queryParams.category reads a quote category equals value quote parameter — and every property on queryParams is a string, or undefined if the caller never sent it at all. That's exactly why a real script checks whether the value exists before calling addQuery with it.

A single Scripted REST API definition can carry many Resources sharing one base path. A GET on one sys_id, a GET listing everything, a POST that creates, a PUT that updates — each of those is its own Resource record with its own focused script. It's not one script branching on the HTTP method; it's separate records, each doing exactly one job.

A developer's-depth script sets the status code that actually matches the outcome. Four hundred signals the caller's request was malformed — a required field missing. Two-oh-one signals a record was actually created, not just a generic two-hundred. Five hundred signals a server-side failure. An integration consuming this API can branch its own error handling on these codes directly.

Every Scripted REST API definition carries its own required-roles setting, configured on the API itself, not on any individual Resource, and not the same thing as a table's ACLs. The platform checks that role requirement before any Resource's script runs at all — a caller without the role never reaches the script. Table ACLs are still a separate layer underneath, inside whatever the script actually queries.

That's the developer's-depth view: query parameters read safely, Resources split by method, real status codes, and a role check that gates the whole API before a script ever runs. Next, versioning — changing a Resource's shape in a new release without breaking the callers still using the old one.
